blocks.x: To open doors to richness in our lives, we each may choose the best of what has gone before, the best of that which lives today, to fashion us a key. And from the minds of those who enter in, this gift is given us, ours still to give and yet to keep. A gift of value great with life itself. And this, our heritage. In this series of heritage programs, we are privileged to meet Mr. Louis Armstrong, the internationally known New Orleans jazz trumpeter and band leader. In this first program, Mr. Armstrong and his guests, Mr. Robert McCulley, writer and publicist, and Mr. Adam Lynch, newscaster, TV personality and classical music broadcaster, discuss Mr. Armstrong's career from his New Orleans boyhood to his present status as a world figure.

Louis, you've been a living legend for so long. For some of us, it gets a little difficult to separate fact from fiction. There are so many stories about you surrounding your life. I'd like to go back, if we could, just a little bit to the beginning. Now, we know New Orleans generally, but specifically, how did you get started? What was it like?

Well, of course, you know, I was born in James Alley. That's back of town, we call it. That's in the rear of the city, where there's one street with everything. Honky tonks, churches, gambling, and everything. And I was just a kid, and I can remember all that. But I never did get heard. Then we moved in to Bedita and Franklin, where there was right to the heart of the little honky tonks, and even a schoolhouse. And we kids going to school didn't pay anything. We used to seeing a lot of loud cats, fights with pistols. It didn't bother you. It didn't even faze us, understand? And finally, I grew up to blow in one of those places myself, which I'm always around music. And I was playing in the honky tonks when Sturerville closed, see? Now, before that, at the age of 12, I was singing in a quartet. I always could sing, because my mother always took my sister and I to church. And this is what they call rock and roll today. We used to hear that same kind of music in sanctified churches, see? But they named it rock and roll, see what I mean? So quite naturally, I always could sing. And I was singing tenor at the time, young man. Put my hand behind my back and tear out, you know. And we'd go around the gamblers and the hustlers and pass our hat, you know, and have us sing for them. Money was money. Yeah, in 1915, a boy 12 years old would bring a dollar and a half of his take home. I would have divided up. That's a lot of money. I could help my sister, my mother, myself, to pay rent and then have a new shirt or new fat shoes or something, you know.
Did the kids you played with think you were about the best that they'd heard?

Well, we wasn't thinking about who was the best or anything in those days. We're just glad we could sing together and sound so good. When did you first start to get there? So when I got to the age where I noticed everybody celebrate Christmas and New Year's Eve with pistols, Roman cannons, shotguns, cannons, anything they got in the processions, they shoot it up there, but I didn't know that there was a law against it. See, you can get away with it, all right, see. Well, I kept on finding my stepfather's old mustard .38 gun, you know, and he had them with blanks in it, but mama kept on hiding it when I'd find it. And I heard this in my bosom one night, and he was going down the right for the street singing, my Brazilian beauty, that was an early tune on Amazon, that's where my love was gone, gone, gone. You know, that face would make that run. How old were you living? Twelve. Yeah. And it's New Year's Eve, coming into 1913, see. So, I was all right till a little kid with a little six-shooter on the other side of the street. Dying, dying, dying, celebrating, you know. So they all know I had this pistol, they say. They call me Dippum out there, get him Dippum. So I just told my big one, he said, yo, yo. Everybody was really good. But when I looked around, those two arms was hugging me, Detective A. Oh, Lord.
Louis, who would you say was the greatest influence on your life? Not in your youth, not musicians, I mean individuals. In your family or?

Well, my mother, she taught us the real things. She always said, you probably never get rich. She was wrong there, wasn't she? Well, she might be. Maybe, you know, maybe $10 million to save $10, you know. But I mean, what she means were have yachts and still got a zillion. We wasn't even thinking about that. She wasn't even thinking about it when she told me, say, but you'll always have health. So take a laxative every night of your life. And that's the finest things you ever told me. You didn't have much money in those days, did you, Louis? Didn't need no money. You didn't need a whole lot because mama could take 15 cents and cook a big pot of red beans and rice and a slice of salt meat and two loaves of bread. The day old for nickel. When did you first hook up with a real orchestra? Well, after I went to the orphanage, we were just shooting a pistol. I had to go to the juvenile court and all that. And I stayed in there for a year and a half. But you played while you were there. Well, how I got into this, second line behind Joe Oliver in the parades. He was always my idol anyway. But I didn't know that about the hard work. Then there was a teacher there by the name of Mr. Peter Davis. It was for a long time before he'd even look at me, you know what I mean? Because from the neighborhood I came from, he figured I was one of them bad boys too, you see? So anyhow, one day Mr. Peter Davis come and he made me the bugler of the institution. And he showed me how to blow the bugle. And watching Joe lift the horn and everything. And I made all the calls. The boys had to drill by my bugle. They had to eat. Get up. Go to sleep. Yeah. And I used to hold that mess call about five minutes late, you know. And them cats all want to kill me. Wish I had a record of some of those calls. Those are the things you said they have tape recorded of. Yeah, that's what I like to have. And finally the little cornet player left in the band and went home. And they put me in the brass band. And that's when I realized the Saints go marching in. Because we used to have to play that every Sunday for the boys to march to church. See? Yeah. And most of my life was right in this institution. And when I got out, I went right into Joe Oliver. So quite naturally he was in my life. I used to run errands for his wife, Miss Stella Oliver. And Joe would give me lessons. And I was always there when she'd give me his red beans and rice. Louie, who else were the musicians around that time that you played with? All of them. Kid Ory, Bunk Johnson. There was Frankie Dooson. Buddy Bowling just left when I was beginning to come out. Because he's the one that blew so loud, he blew himself crazy. See, now I'm a kid watching all this. Kid Ory was quite a player. Always was a good sound man. Good, honest musician. But most of the musicians that didn't take care of themselves would drop bed in the parade in the hot sun around 3 or 4 o'clock in the evening. Too much whiskey and no clean out. When did you start to get recognition across the country as well as just locally? Well, that's one thing I didn't pay any attention about. I never did. It's one of them things. It had to happen. If all the other cats are dropping out and I'm still blowing like I did in the tailgate, I ain't paying no attention of success and all. Because I wasn't worried about that. My success, I played good. And the little money that I didn't make. You know what I mean? I took care of Mama and Mama Lucy. And I didn't have to worry about when am I going to be a big shot or nothing. Because we wasn't taught that everybody was good in New Orleans.
When did you leave New Orleans?

1922. 22. When I went to play second trumpet with Joe Oliver at Lincoln Garden in Chicago. See? How long did you play that? And he was on the other. He was scabbing at that time. But he was such a popular man in Chicago. And he sent for me to play trumpet. And I just had finished a funeral with the Tuxedo Brass Band with Celestan Lita. You know? And they took me to the station trying to tell me, don't go. Because Joe Oliver was scabbing, man. I said, what is scabbing? I don't know.
You didn't even know what it was?
I just want to blow with Joe. I didn't care what Joe was doing. Union rules.
Music was on the other side.

I just want to blow with him. Because I know there wasn't nobody else going to get me out of New Orleans but Joe Oliver. Because I used to see so many of my little friends come back and have to run away from home. They're so hungry and raggedy. Don't have a corner. I said, well, I don't want to do that.
After Oliver, then what?

Well, I stayed with Oliver a long time. See what I mean? After I stayed with Oliver, we got so wedged in together making duets and musicians like Bix and Paul Whiteburn and all them people sitting down. They couldn't understand how we played so well together. When Joe got ready for a break, I had every note to it. And we just sitting right there and didn't say nothing to each other. That's how well I loved them. When did you start recording? When was the first? With Joe Oliver. About 1922. The same time of the New Orleans Rhythm Kings was recording down in Richmond, Indiana for the, what is that, the Ginette record. Now most of Joe's tunes are on the Ginette. And I was a young country boy there, you know, and there were quite nice Joe's fading out. And in those early days, the musicians didn't take care of their teeth and the days of powery, you know, all that number. Well, that was Joe's downfall. Well, quite naturally, he could take his teeth. You couldn't do that. Now I'd play trumpet the way you have to play. See? Well, quite naturally, if I'm going to play second trumpet, I had to get to the door. And we had them horns. They didn't have mics. Joe had to get right up in the mic. Lean right into it. Yeah, because his tone didn't register like Bob Johnson's did. See? And with my tone and strong, I had to get there in order to blend with Joe's. I showed you how to time. I said, now you can stand anywhere and play. You got a mic to catch it. Do you suppose it's easier now for a kid under comparable situations? Much easier. If he'd just gone and take out the idea that if we try to show him something, you know, they'll tell you, well, you're an old man. Yeah. But they ain't thinking about the strategy and as you age up, you know, they're a little kid in my neighborhood. He was so outstanding on bugle in school, you know, neighbor. And I said, well, I'll write and give him a trumpet, which I did. And bought a little method. We had little duets and things. And every time I go to say, now, you see this phrase here. He said, oh, I know that. You know what I mean? Well, I'm a busy man. You know, I ain't got too much time. I already know what he's doing. So I said, now, you just take him on, you know, and enjoy yourself. Because I ain't got time to try to teach somebody that already knew everything. And that's the kids for you nowadays. Do you find that everywhere you go? Well, I don't bother about it. I ain't no teacher. They ask me a question. I keep my lips up and everything. I say, well, a little witch hazel. Never try to jive them and lip salves that we get from Germany. The musician's been buying all the time. It's just guys don't want to be bought because it's greasy or something. But it penetrates and keeps the lips strong. And you have a person. See, one thing I told the youngsters. Okay, great. Your knowledge is I'm a trumpet. You can be a voice to your soul or whatever it is. But if your emphasis is not strong to exercise what you got in mind, you're in trouble. Same as a fighter. If he knock your block off, he get to you. But if them legs don't get him out the way of a punch, what good is it?
When you were talking earlier about your playing with Oliver and Kidore, is there somebody now that's playing with you that you expect in the years to come will move to the forefront?

Well, every musician I have in my band because we don't have but one trumpet. So that means me. Yeah. I expect to do it. You're going to be doing all the movement. Well, that's what I mean. What about other orchestras around here? The mojo. I just got to relax. I know what it is. Just keep my stomach clean out.
What about the other orchestras, the small orchestras around here?

Yeah, a lot of good ones. Now, like any band that plays good. When you say good, you mean... Well, what I mean, I mean, let's throw in a lot of blues and discards. Yeah. Just to get it over with. If you can feel, I mean, and every band that's playing sounds good to me. I got everybody's records. I got from blip to blop. All the way through. Everything. That's the way you're going to appreciate music. Yeah, everybody.

It's been an interesting thing with your career, Louis, that the time that you have become, as I started as a boy, the whole industry, the recording industry has grown. Television has come in, motion pictures. Actually, this has given you a great exposure all over the world now.
Sure. And the first radio when it first started. When I left New Orleans, there was no radio.

A few years ago, you did a movie that I remember particularly because I liked it so much with Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra, High Society. When you do a motion picture like that, do you feel that you're working as a musician or as a performer?

Well, with cats like Bing and Frank, how can you feel other way but just to get together? Because, I mean, even when you got your lines... On this script, every line in there is something that you would say if he was in Chicago or in some joint or something together or some hotel room. You know?
I guess in some of those old radio shows you did with Crosby...

So relax, you know? You didn't always stay to the script entirely all the time, did you? You didn't have to. I mean, how many times... Bing was... One time he was singing... Give me a kiss, then I dream... He said, wait a minute. This is your number. Come on up and sing. And then we did have enough. He's one of the great ad-libbers, isn't he? I mean, he's so natural, you know.
You've worked with a lot of good people, Louie, in your time. Outside of musicians, who are some of the top people you think? I mean, you've worked with Danny Kay, of course.

Yes, Danny Kay and all of them. Just during the time we made five pennants, and he'd be reloading the camera. I'm in his office looking at the World Series ballgame. And then they'd say, all on. Oh, Wenderson, you know Gustav Mahler? Oh, the rock monitor, just that easy. We don't even bother about it. One more time. One more time. See? And I look at them, and they're so great. They run their script down and put it in the pocket and talk about something else. Well, I'm going to do that, too. And Dick Powell was cute when we made Going Places, when he was acting himself, you know. He'd have all his cast around the rehearsal lines, seeing everybody turning praises and whatever. But when he says, da-da-da-da-da-da-da, now look here, man. You've got to do this. What about them? That's the way they start off the rehearsal. You like to work that way? Any kind of way, yeah. But, I mean, that's his way of, boom, getting everybody right in there together. See?

You were talking earlier about the orchestras in the old days and the playing for the funerals and the impromptu stuff on the street corner. Is that being done at all anymore? Who's doing it? Are these names? The younger generation. Are we going to hear from them?

Well, it'll be some down there. But I think they got the wrong idea about things. They want to blow the roof off. All volume and no feeling. Yeah. And then we look around, the chop's tied. Yeah. But in my days coming up, like a man like old man Morett, he was way up in age. See, and there were several trumpet players that instilled things in me and I admired and I never forgot. And most of my education is observing. See, now, there's old man Morett, he had a brass band, oh, about 15, 20 pieces. And every time he wanted to stop that band, he didn't have a note. And he don't strain it on, just look up and just try to do it. And every time he get it. But the Amish youngster wouldn't notice that. Yeah. You know, well, you can't do that all the time. When I come off the plane, the jet plane, I'm carried away with that. Going to Italy and then this palace, that's how I got sick. I carried away with the spaghetti and a bottle of beer. And then I went to sleep in this window and caught cold. And that's why the people in another. About coma, well, that's the first time I heard it was coma. You were talking to me about. But I don't want to cut you off. Go ahead. But I want to show you about Jack Teagarden. We never did worry about when we go to a studio together. We got to do so many minutes and all. Just tell the leader what we want. And it's the same thing. They've been playing, been jamming somewhere. And that's how I act. So when I get off the plane in New York, I drop my bags. I live right by the LaGuardia Airport out in Corona. And I dropped my bags 1.30 that morning and went right down to the round table where Jack was playing and got up on the stand and finished the last hour. See, that's when you love Wonder now. Yeah.
You do it any time. Of the fellows that started out with you, are any of them still around playing?
Yeah.
Kid O'Reilly. Oh, of course. He's still. Fox Foster.

You know what I mean? Well, what about, well, L. Hines is a young one. Yeah. But there ain't a very many that's from that New Orleans guy. No, that's why I'm not. Because most of them are still in New Orleans. They don't want to leave home. And after they come up and stay a while, they get home sick. Well, you know, that's no good.

You were talking about Italy. You've achieved, of course, a great reputation for being sort of an ambassador at large when you go to these various countries. I got a suspicion you really get a kick out of visiting foreign lands, don't you?

Yeah. I tell them, but it's got to be music when they come to the ambassador and things. Because I don't know about politics. You don't care. I just won't blow the horn. So I have them to understand that, which is kicks and coming out with these cutaways and then play one of them old lowdown blues. And the place goes wild.
All these people in these countries have heard you by way of record, haven't they?

Yeah, before you get over there. You know what I mean? And all I can say, we play Marseille. I walk out on the stage, Madame Monsieur, but now, them there eyes. That's all. And that goes over real bad. That's all I do. Because I don't believe in trying to ham up their language. It's not necessary. You know, says a guy come over here and try to speak English, you know, who he's talking about or something. But they're just the little things, a little chuckle, you know. And that's it. Like in Lovey and Rose, when I played the record and going into that instrumental chorus, all I say in that chorus, wee wee. Little things.
Louie, how many tours have you made to Europe now?

Oh, I've been going along about eight or ten times in different times. It was jazz festivals and things. You went over in 32 the first time. First time, 32. Then I would come back, and I went back and stayed over a year or so, and come back in 35. And then from then on, we was going over for different events.
You've played Africa,
Europe.
Have you been to Japan?

Been to Japan. Oh, that's so great. And I mean, like we say, we don't know who's imitating who. Because everywhere you go, somebody has a little idea of something you did. Or you look at them, something they're doing. And I got jazz records from the Japanese musicians. You don't know whether that client plays Benny Goodman or Peanuts or Gold.
What years were they making jazz in Japan? When did they start? The same years we've been doing. They've had jazz all along.

I got all them records, man. I mean, good music. See what I mean? And there's, we go to a nightclub, and there's a Japanese comedian and a Japanese woman comedian, I guess. The other thing Bellman and I do, well, that's my desire. They was doing that with chops and everything. That's cute. What about it? In their language. See what I mean?
Is the recording industry
big over there? Yeah. They're right. Same. They give long playing albums. It's the same.
It's amazing, I think, for us, especially those of us who have not traveled extensively, it's hard for us to realize that jazz has made this tremendous inroad. And it's gone into every country.

It's, listen, man, it's something that nobody can change. I'll tell you why. when Bechet was in Paris playing at a jazz festival one time, Charlie Parker was living there and he was on that bill. So they're going to give Paris something new. But they still got the good old timers there in case something go wrong and good thing they had him. Charlie Parker wouldn't even speak to Bechet coming up or going over on the plane because he's, you know, just going to be here. But Bechet ain't worried about him because he lived in Paris for so many years and France is so near New Orleans and everything, you know what I mean, the language and the cooking. That's right. You know, it's background. Well, the big mistake they made put Bechet on first. Uh-huh. So we just show them the music we've been liking but we're going to give them something new, the old Charlie Parker for last. Well, the only way Charlie Parker could get on after he finished Muscle Red Rambles, he had Lips Page on trumpet, Big Chief on trombone, and, well, you probably want to know all the musicians that, but the next little combo that Bechet had. But when they got through with Muscle Red Rambles and Lips Singing and Blues, Chief is playing starters on the side of his trombone. Do you know how Charlie Parker got on? Then she had to go back stage and hug him and bring him out and plead to the audience to listen to him. That's how great our music is. That's a wonderful story. Yes, sir. Well, it must be... See, those styles of Charlie Parker and Dizzy, don't think that they're not good musicians. They played like everybody else in the old days. But during the jam sessions, these riffs are coming out. See, now you might be sitting there, you're a businessman, so we can take these riffs and call it a style. At least make a lot of money. Which they did. I don't know whether the boppers got anything. They're still walking around with a little hot water bottle.
What about some of the, some of the far out musicians, Louie? Are they saying anything with their music? Are they, are they really talking?

Everywhere you go, there's musicians playing the same thing we playing. And, I'll go you one better. I just told, I was just telling some musicians earlier, all the big bands in America got to tip the hats to all the, the ranger, because, all the rangers, because they're all farmers.
The big bands of the, of the big band era. So, let's think that over. When you're out on a stage in Italy or in France, do you think back of those early days in New Orleans?

No, there wasn't no day to think back. I'm still living them. I still do the same thing. I mean, I eat my meals and I take care of my health and go and blow when I get ready to go to work and warm up and do the same thing.
Is it a treat for you to walk down those streets again? Yeah.
It's a pleasure,
isn't it?

It's wonderful. Half of them tone up, you know, the places, just like Wiley Avenue, all tone up. Well, that's the way it was really. But there's still old Sister Maggie probably down there. Some of the, the old women that probably was young when I was a child. And they would say, come here, boy. I'll raise you. I'd say, okay. I haven't met parents when I was a little kid.
If you had your choice of places to perform, where have you been best received? Where would you like to go?

Everywhere I've been and still going. I play the same right here as I did in Caracas during the time they were supposed to bomb the school, man. And them students sitting in there like they ain't never heard of it. I don't know what they're talking about. I'm just blowing and they didn't drop no bomb. I told the kid, we played for the President's party, everything went good. How many years are you going to be playing? Well, musicians, where I come from, they don't retire, they just stop at any more gigs. So I'm a hustle man. It's fine. The horn, the horn, like you say, the horn ain't killing me. And they ain't what we kill it. I mean, and if I ain't playing one night as I'll be in some of this little spot and Corona there where you just come in and sit down and listen to all the music you want to and pay no admission or nothing, of course, there's a bar there and all, but there'll always be six pieces on the stand and probably I'll just stay right there and blow, you know.

We have been visiting with Mr. Louis Armstrong, internationally known New Orleans jazz trumpeter and band leader, and his guests, Mr. Robert McCulley and Mr. Adam Lynch. In part two of this series, Mr. Armstrong and his guests will discuss his role as an ambassador of goodwill through his travels around the world. This program was produced in the studios of Station WQED in Pittsburgh. And from the minds of those who enter in, this gift is given and this, our heritage. .
